transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. To start, can you tell me what's been bothering you or what brings you in to see me?

Well, they sent me here because of something that happened at the station. I was... I kept moving the airway bags into this pattern. I just knew it was the right way to set them up. And I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud while I did it. 

My lieutenant came over and told me to stop and step away, but I wouldn't do it. I couldn't, really, because it felt like the whole ambulance bay would go bad if I broke the sequence. So... that's why they made me come in to see you.
When you think about it now, do you feel that the idea that something bad would happen if you broke the pattern was unreasonable or excessive, or do you still feel it was actually true?

I... I'm not really sure. It didn't seem unreasonable to me. It just felt like a fact, you know? Like I had to do it. Even now, thinking about it... I don't know if it was excessive. It just felt completely true.
Have you noticed anything unusual lately, like hearing voices or sounds that others don't seem to hear, or seeing things that others don't see?

No, I haven't noticed anything like that. I don't hear voices or see things that aren't there. It's just... the patterns and the numbers, mostly. But no, no voices or anything unusual like you're asking about.
How long have you been doing this kind of pattern-arranging and number-repeating—has it been going on for weeks or months, or did it start suddenly just recently?

Well, the stuff at the station... the bags and the numbers... and before that, I was having some issues with the cameras and my paperwork... all of that has been going on for about the last two months, I'd say. It didn't just start yesterday, but it's been building up over the last couple of months.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient exhibits repetitive, ritualistic behaviors (arranging airway bags in a specific pattern, repeating dispatch numbers) that are time-consuming and cause functional impairment at work. These behaviors are driven by an intrusive belief that failing to perform them will lead to a bad outcome. The patient shows poor insight, being unable to recognize the belief as excessive or unreasonable, but denies any hallucinations or other psychotic symptoms, and there is no evidence of a broader delusional system or thought disorder. The symptoms have been present for about two months, involve compulsive/ritualistic behavior with an obsessive quality (fear of consequences), consistent with Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder with poor insight rather than a primary psychotic disorder.
